title: Zero determinant, squashed space
objectives: Link a zero determinant to a singular matrix and dependent columns.
Tell a singular matrix from one with a merely small determinant.

screens.title: Squash the square
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & d \end{pmatrix}$, so $\det \mathbf{A} = 2d - 1$. Slide $d$ down and watch the parallelogram grow thinner.
screens.question: Slide $d$ until the square is squashed flat.

hints.text: The image is flat when both arrows point along one line.
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, 1)$ is fixed. When is $(1, d)$ on the same line?

feedback.correct: At $d = 0.5$ both arrows lie on one line, and the area is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the $d$ that puts the two arrows on one line.

byKey.zero: At $d = 0$ the second arrow is $(1, 0)$, off the line of $(2, 1)$. The area is still 1.

explain.text: At $d = 0.5$ the second column, $(1, 0.5)$, is half the first, $(2, 1)$. The square collapses onto one line, so its area and $\det \mathbf{A}$ are both 0. Below $0.5$ the determinant turns negative: the square comes back face down.

screens.title: Where can the image go?
screens.prose: Fix $d = 0.5$, so $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. Drag the point $\mathbf{x}$ around the plane. Its image $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ leaves a trail.
screens.question: Where does $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ always land?

options.text: On one line through the origin, $y = x/2$

options.why: Watch the trail: it never leaves one line. Both columns point along $(2, 1)$.
Only some inputs go to the origin. $\mathbf{x} = (1, 1)$ lands at $(3, 1.5)$.

options.text: On the line through $\mathbf{x}$ and the origin
options.why: The image does not follow the direction of $\mathbf{x}$. Move $\mathbf{x}$ in a circle: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ stays on one fixed line.

hints.text: Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to several far-apart places and look at the trail.

feedback.correct: Every image lies on the line $y = x/2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to several places and look at the shape of the trail.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = x_1(2, 1) + x_2(1, 0.5) = (2x_1 + x_2)(1, 0.5)$. Every image is a multiple of $(1, 0.5)$, so the plane is squashed onto the line $y = x/2$. That line is the column space of $\mathbf{A}$.

screens.title: Inputs that vanish
screens.prose: Some inputs land on the origin itself. Now $\mathbf{x}$ has first entry 1 and slides only up and down. $\mathbf{A}$ is still $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$.
screens.question: Drag $\mathbf{x}$ until $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.

hints.text: The first entry of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is $2(1) + x_2$.
$x_2 = -2$. Check the second entry: $1 + 0.5(-2) = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make both entries of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ zero: $2 + x_2 = 0$.

byKey.half: You set $x_2 = -0.5$. The first entry is then $2 - 0.5 = 1.5$, not 0.
byKey.X: Not there yet. The first entry of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is $2 + x_2$, so it must be 0.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}(1, -2) = 1 \cdot (2, 1) - 2 \cdot (1, 0.5) = (0, 0)$. Two inputs, $\mathbf{0}$ and $(1, -2)$, share the output $\mathbf{0}$, so nothing can undo $\mathbf{A}$. A square matrix with no inverse is **singular**.

screens.title: Three columns, one plane
screens.prose: In three dimensions a zero determinant squashes space flat. $\mathbf{B}$ has $\det \mathbf{B} = 0$, and its third column is a mix of the other two.
screens.question: Find $p$ and $q$ with column 3 $= p \times$ column 1 $+ q \times$ column 2.

hints.text: Down each row the entries go up in equal steps: 1, 2, 3.
Column 2 $-$ column 1 $= (1, 1, 1)$, and so does column 3 $-$ column 2.
Column 3 $=$ column 2 $+ (1, 1, 1) = 2 \times$ column 2 $-$ column 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the top row first: $3 = p + 2q$. Then check the second row.

byKey.r0c1: Check the top row: $3 = p \times 1 + q \times 2$. With $q = 2$ that needs $p = -1$.

explain.text: $-1 \cdot (1, 4, 7) + 2 \cdot (2, 5, 8) = (3, 6, 9)$. So the three columns span only a plane. $\mathbf{B}$ squashes all of space onto that plane, and volume goes to 0.

screens.title: Tune one entry
screens.prose: One entry of $\mathbf{C}$ is free. Expand along row 1 to find $\det \mathbf{C}$ in terms of $k$.
screens.question: For which $k$ is $\mathbf{C}$ singular?

hints.text: Expand along row 1: $1 \cdot M_{11} - 2 \cdot M_{12} + 0$.
$\det \mathbf{C} = (k - 1) - 2(-2) = k + 3$. Set it to 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand along row 1 with the signs $+, -, +$, then set the result to 0.

byKey.nosign: You added the middle term. With its minus sign, $-2(0 - 2) = +4$, so $\det \mathbf{C} = k + 3$.
byKey.first: You kept only the first term, $k - 1$. The middle term adds 4.

explain.text: $\det \mathbf{C} = 1(k - 1) - 2(0 - 2) + 0 = k + 3$, which is 0 at $k = -3$. Then column 3 is $(0, 1, -3)$, which equals column 2 minus twice column 1. Dependent columns appear exactly when the determinant hits 0.

screens.title: Small is not singular
screens.prose: $\mathbf{S} = 0.001\,\mathbf{I}$ has $\det \mathbf{S} = 10^{-6}$. $\mathbf{N} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.0001 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\det \mathbf{N} = 10^{-4}$, a hundred times larger.

state.caption: Left: the image under $\mathbf{S}$, zoomed in 1000 times. Right: the image under $\mathbf{N}$, beside the dashed unit square.

screens.question: Which matrix is closer to squashing the plane flat?

options.why: You compared the determinants. $\mathbf{S}$ shrinks evenly and keeps a perfect square, and $\mathbf{S}^{-1} = 1000\,\mathbf{I}$ undoes it exactly.

options.text: $\mathbf{N}$, since its columns almost line up

options.why: Both are invertible, but not equally safe. Change $\mathbf{N}$'s 1.0001 to 1 and it is singular.

hints.text: Look at the shapes, not the sizes.
$\mathbf{N}$'s columns are $(1, 1)$ and $(1, 1.0001)$.
A tiny nudge makes $\mathbf{N}$'s columns equal. No tiny nudge flattens a square.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how small a change would make each matrix singular.

byKey.smaller: You read a small determinant as nearly singular. Scaling all entries by 0.001 scales the determinant by $10^{-6}$ but keeps the shape.

explain.text: $\mathbf{S}$'s image is still a square, only small, so $\mathbf{S}$ is easy to undo. $\mathbf{N}$'s columns point almost the same way, so its image is a sliver. The honest measure is the **condition number**: 1 for $\mathbf{S}$, about 40,000 for $\mathbf{N}$.

screens.prose: For a square matrix $\mathbf{A}$, these all say the same thing: $$\det \mathbf{A} = 0$$ The columns are dependent. $\mathbf{A}$ squashes space into fewer dimensions. $\mathbf{A}$ has no inverse. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has a solution $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}$.
screens.question: $\det \mathbf{M} = 0$ for a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{M}$. Which follow? Select all that apply.

options.why: The image is at most a plane, so most $\mathbf{b}$ are out of reach.
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ has no zero entry, yet its determinant is $4 - 4 = 0$. The same happens in $3 \times 3$.

hints.text: A zero determinant means space is squashed. What can and cannot be reached?
Dependent columns, a non-zero input sent to $\mathbf{0}$, and no inverse all follow. Reaching every $\mathbf{b}$ does not.

feedback.correct: Dependent columns, a non-zero solution of $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, and no inverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A zero determinant is about the columns as a whole, not single entries.

explain.text: A zero determinant means the columns are dependent, so some $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}$ goes to $\mathbf{0}$ and no inverse exists. The image is a plane or smaller, so most $\mathbf{b}$ are unreachable. Entries can all be non-zero.

screens.title: Parallel columns give zero
screens.prose: Why do dependent columns force a zero? In $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$, suppose column 2 is $t$ times column 1: $b = ta$ and $d = tc$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

hints.text: Start from the formula, before substituting anything.
Replace $d$ and $b$ next.
Formula, substitute, reorder, cancel.

feedback.correct: Parallel columns make the two products equal, so they cancel.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $ad - bc$, substitute, then simplify.

explain.text: With $b = ta$ and $d = tc$, both products equal $tac$, so $ad - bc = 0$. In pictures: the two arrows lie on one line, and the parallelogram has no area.

screens.title: A riskless pair
screens.prose: Stocks A and B have annual volatilities of 20% and 30%, with correlation 1. Their covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is shown, and $\det \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = 0.0036 - 0.0036 = 0$.
screens.question: You hold £3,000 of A. How much of B should you sell short to leave no risk?

widget.label: Amount of B to short, in £

hints.text: With correlation 1, the two stocks move in lockstep, scaled by their volatilities.
A £1 position in A carries risk 0.2; in B, 0.3.
Match the risks: $0.2 \times 3000 = 0.3 \times x$.

feedback.correct: £2,000 short of B cancels the £600 of risk in A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the risk of the two positions: volatility times amount.

byKey.same: Equal amounts leave B's larger swings uncovered. Match the risks: $0.2 \times 3000 = 0.3 \times x$.
byKey.inverted: You scaled by $0.3/0.2$, the wrong way round. B is the more volatile stock, so you need less of it.

explain.text: Risk matches when $0.2 \times 3000 = 0.3 \times x$, so $x = \text{£}2{,}000$. The positions $(3000, -2000)$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$, so the portfolio variance is 0. An optimiser that inverts $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ breaks here: it sees a riskless trade and, if the returns differ, scales it without limit.

ideas: $\det \mathbf{A} = 0$ exactly when the columns are dependent: the plane is squashed onto a line, or space onto a plane.
Then $\mathbf{A}$ has no inverse, and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has solutions with $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}$.
A small determinant is not a warning on its own: $0.001\,\mathbf{I}$ is perfectly invertible. The condition number measures closeness to singular.

formula.name: Singular matrix
formula.note: Equivalently: dependent columns, no inverse, squashed space.

summary.trap: A tiny determinant can come from shrinking everything evenly. Nearly parallel columns, not a small number, make a matrix nearly singular.

options.text: $\mathbf{A}$ has an inverse, because no entry is 0
options.why: Zero entries do not decide it. $2 \times 3 - 6 \times 1 = 0$, so there is no inverse.

options.text: $\mathbf{A}$ squashes the plane to a single point
options.why: Its columns are not zero, so the image is a whole line, not a point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two columns, then compute $ad - bc$.

explain.text: Column 2, $(6, 3)$, is 3 times column 1, $(2, 1)$. So $\det \mathbf{A} = 2 \times 3 - 6 \times 1 = 0$, and $\mathbf{A}$ squashes the plane onto the line through $(2, 1)$.

options.why: You took the positive root only. $(-2)^2 - 4 = 0$ as well.
You set $k$ equal to the 4. The determinant is $k^2 - 4$, which is 12 at $k = 4$.
$\det \mathbf{A} = k^2 - 4$ does reach 0, at two values.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\det \mathbf{A}$ in terms of $k$ and set it to 0.

explain.text: $\det \mathbf{A} = k \cdot k - 4 \cdot 1 = k^2 - 4$. It is 0 when $k^2 = 4$, so at $k = 2$ and at $k = -2$.

quiz.prose: Every column of $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$ is a multiple of $(1, 2, 3)$.
quiz.question: What does $\mathbf{B}$ squash space onto?

options.why: A zero determinant allows a plane, but here every column lies along $(1, 2, 3)$. The image is that one line.
Only the zero matrix sends everything to one point. $\mathbf{B}$'s columns are not zero.

feedback.correct: All columns lie along $(1, 2, 3)$, so the image is a line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The image is everything the columns can reach together.

explain.text: Columns 2 and 3 are 2 and 3 times column 1. Every $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}$ is a multiple of $(1, 2, 3)$, so space is squashed onto that line. A zero determinant only says the image is flat; it can be a plane, a line or a point.

options.why: A determinant is not a closeness score. $\mathbf{T}$ shrinks every direction evenly, and $100\,\mathbf{I}$ undoes it exactly.

options.text: Only if $10^{-6}$ is above some cut-off
options.why: Any non-zero determinant means an inverse exists. How safe it is to compute depends on the condition number, which is 1 here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether some matrix undoes $\mathbf{T}$.

explain.text: $\det \mathbf{T} = 0.01^3 = 10^{-6}$, which is small but not 0. $\mathbf{T}$ shrinks every direction by 100, and $100\,\mathbf{I}$ undoes it. Its condition number is 1, the best possible.
